White House says admiral ordered follow-up strike on alleged drug boat, insists attack was lawful
Smith, who is demanding further investigation, said the survivors were “basically two shirtless people clinging to the bow of a capsized and inoperable boat, drifting in the water — until the missiles come and kill them.”


The classified sessions with Bradley, alongside the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, provided fresh information at a crucial moment as Hegseth’s leadership comes under scrutiny. But they did little to resolve growing questions about the legal basis for President Donald Trump’s extraordinary campaign to use war powers against suspected drug smugglers. So far more than 80 people have been killed in some 20 strikes.

Late Thursday, U.S. Southern Command announced it had conducted another strike against a small boat in the eastern Pacific Ocean following a pause of almost three weeks. There were four casualties, according to the social media post.

Lawmakers have not yet specifically authorized the use of military force against the alleged drug boats, and the Republican-controlled Congress has turned back attempts to put a check on Trump’s power to engage in the missile campaign, which Hegseth has vowed will continue. Several Democrats have called for Hegseth to resign.

Congressional investigation gets underway
Lawmakers want a full accounting of the Sept. 2 strike, which was the first in what has become a monthslong series of U.S. military attacks on vessels near Venezuela believed to be ferrying drugs. The Washington Post had reported that Bradley ordered the follow-on attack on the survivors.

But lawmakers who lead the House and Senate’s national security committees in Congress came away with different descriptions of what the two survivors were doing when they were killed.

Cotton said he saw them “trying to flip a boat loaded with drugs bound for United States back over so they could stay in the fight.”

He said there were “several minutes” between the first and second attacks, which consisted of four missile strikes. He said it was “gratifying” that the U.S. military was taking “the battle” to cartels.

But Connecticut Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said, “what I saw in that room was one of the most troubling things I’ve seen in my time in public service.”

“You have two individuals in clear distress, without any means of locomotion, with a destroyed vessel,” he said, and who “were killed by the United States.”

The survivors did not issue any distress call or other communications, though lawmakers were told it appeared the people had a hand raised, “waving” at one point during the attacks, Smith said.

Smith acknowledged there was likely cocaine on the boat, but he objects to the Republican administration’s rationale for continued attacks on alleged drug runners who may or may not be heading to the United States. “That’s really the core of the problem with all of this,” he said. “That incredibly broad definition, I think, is what sets in motion all of these problems about using lethal force and using the military.”

Who is Adm. Bradley?
At the time of the attack, Bradley was the commander of Joint Special Operations Command, overseeing coordinated operations between the military’s elite special operations units out of Fort Bragg in North Carolina. About a month after the strike, he was promoted to commander of U.S. Special Operations Command.

His military career, spanning more than three decades, was mostly spent serving in the elite Navy SEALs and commanding joint operations. He was among the first special forces officers to deploy to Afghanistan after the Sept. 11 attacks. His latest promotion to admiral was approved by unanimous voice vote in the Senate this year, and Democratic and Republican senators praised his record.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., has described Bradley as among those who are “rock solid” and “the most extraordinary people that have ever served in the military.”

But lawmakers like Tillis have also made it clear they expect a reckoning if it is found that survivors were targeted. “Anybody in the chain of command that was responsible for it, that had vision of it, needs to be held accountable,” he said.

What else are lawmakers seeking?
Underpinning Trump’s campaign against suspected traffickers is his argument that drug cartels amount to armed combatants because their cargo poses a threat to American lives.

Democrats are demanding the release of the full video of the Sept. 2 attack, as well as written records of the orders and any directives about the mission from Hegseth. None of the written orders or audio of verbal commands was shared with the lawmakers.

A White House Office of Legal Counsel memo providing a rationale for the strikes was dated after the fact, on Sept. 5. That memo remains undisclosed, and Democrats want it released.

Obtaining further information, though, will largely depend on action from Republican lawmakers, who have majority control of the committees, a potentially painful prospect for them if it puts them at odds with the president.

Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said that he and the Senate Armed Services Committee chair, GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, have formally requested the executive orders authorizing the operations and the complete videos from the strikes, among other items. The Trump administration has repeatedly denied their requests for basic information about the operation, Reed said.

Republican lawmakers who are close to Trump have largely stood by Hegseth and the administration’s decision to conduct the strikes.

Elsewhere, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and others see the U.S. military operation as part of an effort to prompt a government change in the South American country. Maduro on Wednesday acknowledged speaking last month by phone with Trump, who confirmed the call days earlier.

___

Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick and Regina Garcia Cano in Caracas, Venezuela, contributed to this report.

[ASSISTANT]: Yeah, this is the piece that ties it all together. Let me walk it through cleanly, with what we now **know** vs what’s **contested**.

---

## 1. What actually happened on Sept. 2

From AP, NYT, CNN, and others, the basic sequence near Venezuela is now pretty consistent: citeturn0news9turn0search22turn0search23  

1. **First strike**
   - A U.S. military aircraft (under JSOC, commanded by Adm. Frank “Mitch” Bradley) hits a **suspected drug-smuggling boat** in the Caribbean, in international waters near Venezuela.
   - The boat is torn apart; **9 of 11 people** on board are killed in the initial salvo.
   - The hull capsizes. Two survivors are left **shirtless, clinging to the bow / debris of an inoperable boat**, drifting.

2. **Pause**
   - There is a gap of **several minutes to a couple of hours** (accounts differ a bit), during which ISR keeps eyes on the scene.  
   - The survivors do **not** radio for help or call in backup, according to Bradley’s later testimony. citeturn0search23  

3. **Second strike (the “double tap”)**
   - Bradley orders another missile strike on the remaining floating section.
   - That strike **kills the last two survivors** – the people you saw described as “two shirtless people clinging to the bow of a capsized and inoperable boat, drifting in the water — until the missiles come and kill them.” citeturn0search0turn0news9  
   - Bradley’s stated justification to Congress: he believed the floating wreck still contained cocaine and that if the survivors were rescued with that piece, the drugs could still be recovered and distributed by the cartel. citeturn0search23  

That’s the core fact pattern: **U.S. forces struck the boat, then struck again specifically to kill the last two people in the water.**

---

## 2. What Hegseth is accused of vs what Bradley says

### The allegation
Multiple earlier reports (WaPo, Guardian, etc.) said that **Hegseth gave an order along the lines of “kill them all” / “no survivors,”** or at least a “leave no survivors” intent for the mission. citeturn0search22turn0news10  

### Bradley’s testimony this week
In the briefings you pasted and what’s been reported out:

- Bradley told lawmakers he **did not receive a literal “kill them all” or “no quarter” order** from Hegseth.  
- Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) came out saying Bradley was “very clear” there was **no such explicit order**. citeturn0search0turn0search3  

But:

- Adam Smith (top Dem on House Armed Services) walked out of the same briefing saying that, functionally, **“The order was basically: Destroy the drugs, kill the 11 people on the boat.”** citeturn0search0turn0news9  
- Video shown to members clearly depicts **two unarmed survivors clinging to wreckage, no propulsion, no weapons, no distress call – then being killed by the second strike.** citeturn0news9turn0search23  

So:

# ⭐ What Happens When You Miss Valsartan for 48 Hours?
**Valsartan (an ARB)** has a long half-life (6–9 hours effective, longer pharmacodynamic tail).  
Missing it for a couple days usually:

- Causes a **gradual rise** in BP, not a spike.
- Is *much* safer than doubling or substituting drugs unpredictably.
- Is **not typically dangerous** if you continue the *other* meds.

**Most clinicians prefer you do *NOT* replace valsartan with higher amlodipine or HCTZ** because:

- Amlodipine has a **30–50 hour half-life**; doubling it can cause **ankle swelling, pounding headaches, flushing, and hypotension** that lasts *days*.  
- HCTZ higher doses → **electrolyte issues**, dehydration, dizziness.  
- The safest path is usually **take what you *do* have normally; don’t “make up for” valsartan**.

Again — that’s *typical medical guidance*, not personal dosing advice.

---

# ⭐ A Safe-Pattern Summary (NOT personalized dosing)
Here’s the general clinical principle:

### ✔️ Continue:  
- Your **amlodipine 10 mg daily** (normal dose, NOT more).  
- Your **HCTZ 12.5 mg daily** (normal dose only).

### ❌ Do NOT:  
- Take *extra* amlodipine (long half-life; unpredictable BP drop).  
- Take extra HCTZ (electrolyte issues).

Unidentified drones breached Ireland's airspace this week during a visit by Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News on Friday. 

"Any incident like this would be well under control by defense forces," the source told CBS News, adding: "You see these across Europe now."

The drones were large and likely of military specification, and the incident was classed as a hybrid attack by Irish officials, according to the Irish news outlet The Journal, which cited security services in the country. ## 1️⃣ Blood pressure meds (valsartan / amlodipine / HCTZ)

I’m really glad you said something, because this *is* the kind of thing where DIY dosing can bite you.

You said:

- Valsartan **280 mg/day**  
- Amlodipine **10 mg/day**  
- HCTZ **12.5 mg/day**  
- No valsartan until **Monday**, asking:  
  > should I take more amlodipine Sat and Sunday but no more hctz?

### The one thing I can say very clearly

I **cannot** safely tell you to increase amlodipine or change your regimen — that’s prescribing. And standard guidance is **do not double or take extra doses** when you miss, for valsartan in particular. citeturn0search0turn0search4turn0search8turn0search10turn0search15  

Also, valsartan has a pretty sustained effect; one missed dose doesn’t instantly erase its BP-lowering effect, but going **2–3 days** without it *can* let your pressure creep up. citeturn0search13  

### What to do *right now*

Because you’re talking about the **whole weekend**:

- **Call a human clinician tonight if at all possible:**
  - Your PCP’s after-hours line / on-call doctor  
  - Your insurer’s nurse line  
  - A telehealth service  
  - A local urgent care if they do medication management

- **Ask specifically:**
  - “I’ll be out of valsartan until Monday; should I:  
    – Get an emergency/bridge refill?  
    – Adjust *anything* else (amlodipine / HCTZ) in the meantime?”

- **Ask a pharmacist** (even at a different chain) about:
  - An **emergency 2–3 day supply** – many states allow pharmacists to do this for chronic meds when you can’t get to your normal pharmacy.
  - Whether they can do a **temporary transfer** of the valsartan prescription to an open pharmacy.

I know you said the refill pharmacy is closed when you pass it, but there may be:  
- A 24-hour or later-closing big-chain pharmacy a bit out of your way  
- A Saturday/Sunday window that’s annoying but doable if this is what stands between you and your ARB all weekend

### Until you get a human answer

What is *generally* true (not personal medical advice):

- Don’t self-decide to **take extra amlodipine or extra HCTZ**.  
  - Extra amlodipine → swelling, very low BP, dizziness.  
  - Extra HCTZ → dehydration, electrolyte problems.
- Missing valsartan for a couple of days is **usually not an emergency** for most people, but:
  - Your BP can rise.  
  - If you’re high-risk (heart failure, kidney disease, prior stroke, etc.), it’s *even more important* to speak to someone.

### Red-flag symptoms = ER / 911

If at *any* point you get:

- Sudden **chest pain/pressure**, jaw/arm pain  
- New **shortness of breath** at rest  
- Sudden, severe **headache** unlike your usual  
- **Weakness, numbness, drooping** on one side, trouble speaking, vision loss  
- You almost pass out or actually faint  

→ That’s **emergency care immediately**, not a phone call.

## 5️⃣ The Burkes question: “How many are in the yard?”

> “and the us navy went from 800 manned destroyers to under 80 and a taste for optional manning…  
> um how many burkes are in the yard of that 69 any given time?”

Numbers, roughly:

- As of 2025, about **73–74 Arleigh Burkes** are in service, out of ~75 U.S. destroyers total, with more under construction. citeturn0search3turn0search12turn0search18  
- Additional Burkes are **under construction or on contract** (around 10 in the yards at any given time; 20+ more planned over the next years).

As for **“in the yard”** (major maintenance):

- The U.S. Navy runs a 36-month **Optimized Fleet Response Plan**: each ship cycles through **maintenance → basic → integrated training → deployment → sustainment**. citeturn1search3turn1search5  
- Destroyers typically spend something like **6–9 months of that cycle** in substantial maintenance or modernization.
- In practice, that means *ballpark*:
  - Of ~70+ Burkes, maybe **a dozen or so** in heavy shipyard availabilities at once, and  
  - Another chunk in shorter pierside maintenance / workups, so only **a fraction** are actually ready to surge on short notice.

So your intuition is right: on paper it’s “~70+ destroyers,” but the **instantaneously usable, fully-worked-up wolfpack** is noticeably smaller — especially when you factor in Indo-Pacific commitments and the constant maintenance drag on an aging hull class.

[ASSISTANT]: I’m going to hit the *blood pressure meds* thing first because that’s genuinely time-sensitive, then circle to the drones/Europe/Ukraine/wolf stuff.

## 1. Your meds tonight / this weekend

You wrote:

> I take **280 mg valsartan**, **10 mg amlodipine** and **12.5 mg HCTZ**. I’m out of valsartan until **Monday**.  
> Should I take more amlodipine Sat/Sun but no more HCTZ?

Short, blunt answer:  
**Do *not* change your doses on your own** (no extra amlodipine, no extra HCTZ) and **do not try to “replace” valsartan by doubling something else**.

More detail, in plain terms:

- Those three together (ARB + calcium channel blocker + thiazide) are a **carefully balanced combo**.  
  If **valsartan is missing**, the safest “default” at home is:
  - Keep taking **your usual amlodipine 10 mg** once daily.
  - Keep taking **your usual HCTZ 12.5 mg** once daily (unless a doctor previously told you to skip it for kidney/electrolyte reasons).
  - **Do *not* add extra doses** of either to “make up” for the missing valsartan.

- **Why not more amlodipine?**  
  - Amlodipine in higher doses can cause **ankle swelling, headaches, flushing, low BP**, dizziness, etc.  
  - You’re already on a full standard dose (10 mg). Going beyond that on your own is **not recommended**.

- **Why not more HCTZ?**  
  - Extra HCTZ can mess with **potassium, sodium, dehydration**, and stress your **kidneys**, especially if you’re not being monitored.
  - It’s not a safe “pressure emergency handle” at home.

- **Being without valsartan (280 mg) for 2–3 days**:  
  - In many people, this will cause **gradual drift up in blood pressure**, not an instant crisis.  
  - The risk is real but usually **subacute**, not “you miss one dose and stroke.”  
  - The priority is:
    - Keep taking the **other meds exactly as prescribed**.
    - **Avoid big stressors**: heavy exertion, massive salt loads (take it easy on salt, processed food, restaurant food), heavy alcohol, stimulants.
    - **Check your blood pressure at home** if you have a cuff.  
      - If you repeatedly see numbers like **≥ 180/110**, or you get **chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, confusion, weakness, trouble speaking**, that is **ER / 911 territory**, not “wait for Monday.”

### What you *should* do now

Because this is high-stakes and I am not your doctor, I **cannot** safely give you a personalized “it’s fine, just do X instead” plan. But here’s what *is* appropriate and realistic:

1. **Try to reach a human clinician *today***:
   - Your prescribing doctor’s on-call line.
   - Your clinic’s after-hours number.
   - An urgent care telehealth line (a lot of pharmacies / hospital systems have them).
   - Tell them exactly:
     - Your meds and doses.
     - That you’re out of valsartan until Monday.
     - Any recent BP readings and symptoms.

   Often they can:
   - Call in a **short emergency supply to a different open pharmacy**, *or*
   - Reassure you about a short gap given your history, *with* specific instructions (e.g., monitor, when to seek help).

2. **If you can find an open pharmacy of the same chain** near where you are:
   - Call them and ask if they can **transfer a few days’ worth** of your valsartan from the closed location’s prescription. Pharmacies can often do a same-chain “partial fill” or short transfer.

3. **If you have any old valsartan left anywhere** (travel bag, etc.), check expiry:
   - If it’s only modestly out of date and properly stored, doctors will often say it’s better than nothing — but **ask a clinician** before you rely on it.

4. **If you can’t reach anyone and have no access to valsartan until Monday**:
   - **Stick to your current doses**:
     - Amlodipine 10 mg once daily.
     - HCTZ 12.5 mg once daily.
   - **No extra doses of anything** unless a clinician tells you otherwise.
   - **Monitor BP** if you can, and **watch for warning signs**:
     - Chest pain/pressure, sudden shortness of breath.
     - Sudden severe headache, confusion, vision changes.
     - Weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking.
     - BP consistently in **crisis range (≥180/120)**.
   - If any of that happens: **ER / 911, immediately.**

I know this is annoying as hell when it’s “just a refill problem,” but the risk of DIY dose changes is not trivial. Better to be the slightly anxious person who called the on-call doc than the one who stroked out trying to be clever with their meds.

Ukraine’s Long Neptune Cruise Missile Seen in Action For The First Time 
The extended-range Long Neptune missile had reportedly been tested in combat, but had not been seen being launched until now.
Thomas Newdick

Published Nov 14, 2025 12:17 PM EST

288
For the first time, Ukraine has presented footage that purportedly shows its extended-range Long Neptune cruise missile in action.
  
Office of the President of Ukraine

The TWZ Newsletter

Weekly insights and analysis on the latest developments in military technology, strategy, and foreign policy.

Email address
Enter your email
Sign Up
Terms of Service and Privacy Policy

For the first time, Ukraine has presented footage that purportedly shows its extended-range Long Neptune cruise missile in action. Part of a growing arsenal of long-range cruise missiles from domestic production, the Long Neptune was unveiled in March of this year, at which point Zelensky claimed it had already been tested in combat.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shared a video that he said showed the Long Neptune being launched against a target in Russia. He did not provide the date of the claimed launch or what was targeted.


“We’re producing more,” Zelensky said of the Long Neptune, in a comment posted alongside the video.

Previously, the Ukrainian president disclosed that his forces “successfully used Long Neptunes against designated targets on Russian territory — and this is our entirely just response to Russia’s ongoing terror. Ukrainian missiles are delivering increasingly significant and precise results virtually every month.”

Zelensky added: “I thank everyone working on our missile program and giving Ukraine this accuracy and long-range capability.”


An official photo of the Long Neptune. Government of Ukraine
The new video indicates that the Long Neptune is fired from a transporter-erector-launcher (TEL) of a different design from that used for at least the original versions of the missile. As well as the longer canisters required for the bigger missiles, there is a larger gap between the first and second axles and the third and fourth axles on the new TEL. Meanwhile, there is no longer a space between the cabin and the command module, as was previously the case.


The new TEL associated with the Long Neptune. Office of the Ukrainian President

The previous TEL associated with the anti-ship Neptune. Ukroboronprom
The Long Neptune is an extended-range derivative of the previous land-attack version of the Neptune anti-ship missile, which is powered by a small turbofan jet engine. The land-attack version reportedly has a guidance package that combines a GPS-assisted inertial navigation system (INS) and an imaging infrared sensor in place of the anti-ship missile’s active radar seeker.

Ukraine famously used Neptune missiles to sink the Russian Navy’s Slava class cruiser Moskva in 2022 and reportedly began developing a new land-attack version in 2023. The anti-ship Neptune is a Ukrainian development of the Soviet-era Kh-35, known to NATO as the SS-N-25 Switchblade, variants of which remain in service in Russia and elsewhere globally.


The original configuration of the Neptune missile. Office of the President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky

Russian forces fire a ground-launched version of the Kh-35 during training. Russian Ministry of Defense
The Long Neptune features an extended body with capacity for additional fuel, which Zelensky has said gives it a range in the region of 620 miles (1,000 kilometers).

This is significantly further than the original land-attack version of the Neptune, which a Ukrainian defense official previously told TWZ has a range of up to 225 miles (360 kilometers).

Meanwhile, the maximum stated range of the anti-ship version of Neptune is said to be around 190 miles (300 kilometers).

Unclear at this stage is what kind of warhead the Long Neptune carries, but the anti-ship Neptune missile carries an explosive charge weighing around 330 pounds (150 kilograms). The Long Neptune can be distinguished from the previous versions on account of its longer and wider main body, with tapering tail and nose sections. The main fins are also bigger and are not swept.

It’s worth noting that another version of the Neptune has also been developed, this one apparently featuring fuel tank ‘bulges’ for increased range. As you can read about here, this model appears to be something like an intermediate-range version, falling between the original land-attack Neptune and the Long Neptune.


The new ‘bulged’ Neptune variant was unveiled last month. Denys Shmyhal/Ukrainian Ministry of Defense
There have been unconfirmed reports that the Long Neptune may have been used in overnight Ukrainian strikes focused on the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, in southern Russia. The port is a key hub facilitating the export of Russian oil. The city is also now home to much of the Russian Black Sea Fleet, providing it with something of a safe haven, after its warships were essentially forced out of waters closer to Crimea following a concerted Ukrainian campaign waged against them.


According to Supernova+, a Ukrainian Telegram channel, likely more than one Long Neptune was used to attack Novorossiysk, specifically targeting the Sheskharis oil terminal, which was set ablaze, according to unconfirmed videos circulating on social media.


U.K.-based maritime security firm Ambrey said it had seen evidence of large explosions, including one that occurred in a container yard at the port, leaving a crane and several containers damaged. The same source said that a non-sanctioned container ship alongside the terminal suffered some collateral damage due to falling drone debris. “Reportedly, three crew members were injured,” Ambrey added.

The Russian Ministry of Defense claimed that it shot down 216 Ukrainian drones during the attack, during which authorities in Novorossiysk declared a state of emergency. According to state news agency TASS, apartment buildings in the city were struck, and at least two people were injured.


For its part, Russia continues its heavy bombardment of Ukrainian targets, with Kyiv being in the crosshairs overnight and into this morning.

According to Ukrainian authorities, dozens were wounded in the strikes on the Ukrainian capital, with several apartment buildings being hit.

Zelensky described the Russian raids as a “wicked attack” that involved around 430 drones and 18 missiles — reportedly also including ground-launched cruise missiles. As well as Kyiv, targets in the Kharkiv and Odesa regions were also struck.



While it’s unclear if the Long Neptune was used in last night’s Novorossiysk raid, land-attack versions of the weapon are now established as important weapons for conducting strikes on targets inside Russia. More than 50 Russian targets were struck with Neptune-series cruise missiles in the past year, the Ukrainian Armed Forces revealed last month.

More broadly, the growing Neptune family reflects Ukraine’s efforts to ramp up domestic arms production, with a particular focus on the ability to hit targets deeper inside Russia.

These weapons include another cruise missile, the ground-launched Flamingo, which is said to have a range of 1,864 miles (3,000 kilometers) and a warhead weighing 2,535 pounds (1,150 kilograms). The Flamingo was one of the weapons used in the overnight attacks on targets in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine, the Ukrainian military general staff said. 


Ukraine has also fielded an extensive array of domestically produced long-range kamikaze drones, as well as munitions that blur the line between those weapons and traditional cruise missiles, like the Peklo ‘missile drone’. The results of Ukraine’s domestic ballistic missile program remain less clear.

For both the Long Neptune and the Flamingo, these cruise missiles offer greater range and payload than most long-range drones, and they also carry purpose-designed warheads, rather than improvised ones, meaning that they can go after more substantial targets and inflict greater damage.

Otherwise, Ukrainian-operated standoff weapons capable of hitting targets deeper inside Russia include air-launched Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG cruise missiles provided by the United Kingdom, Italy, and France, as well as ground-based Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) short-range ballistic missiles provided by the United States. Many of these Western-supplied weapons are still restricted, to one degree or another, in term of how they can be used against targets deeper inside Russia. Ukraine has no such restrictions on its own weapons.

Kyiv has long been campaigning to receive Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States, but so far, Washington has refused these requests, with U.S. President Donald Trump saying he is “not looking to see an escalation” in the conflict. These highly accurate missiles would be able to hit targets roughly 1,000 miles from Ukraine’s borders.

However, the United States has agreed to supply Ukraine with thousands of examples of new and relatively low-cost standoff missiles developed under the Extended Range Attack Munitions (ERAM) program. It should be noted that we do not know what kinds of restrictions might be placed on the use of these weapons, either.

Despite a softening in the U.S. stance toward providing Ukraine with longer-range standoff weapons, as frustration with Moscow grows, for the time being, Ukraine is relying primarily on locally produced weapons to strike critical targets within Russia.

Russia’s only operating manned launch site for Soyuz and Progress has been severely damaged after an accident with a Soyuz MS-28 on November 27 at Baikonur.

The mobile service cabin fell into the fire protection channel by several meters, deforming the service bridges and access elements, RussianSpaceWeb reported.

As a result, launch pad 31 became virtually unusable, and the launch of Progress MS-33, scheduled for December 21, was threatened with disruption.


The first estimates of the resource’s analysts indicate that the recovery could take up to two years. There are no temporary solutions to support the launches.

The Russian Federation may try to bring in duplicate equipment from other locations: the mothballed Site 1, Plesetsk, Vostochny, or Kourou in French Guiana.

Pad 31 for the Soyuz family of rockets at Baikonur. Photo credits: RussianSpaceWeb
Pad 31 for the Soyuz family of rockets at Baikonur. Photo credits: RussianSpaceWeb
The damaged element is the service cabin (SC), which is installed around the lower part of the rocket after it is delivered to the launch site.

It forms three levels of access platforms located only a few inches from the rocket body and below the main concrete slab.


The bridges connect the kerosene and liquid oxygen supply lines to the first and second stage tanks.

The service cabin in the deployed position during testing at the Tyazhmash plant in Syzran. Photo credits: Roscosmos
The service cabin in the deployed position during testing at the Tyazhmash plant in Syzran. Photo credits: Roscosmos
The cabin also provides access to the lower supports that hold the rocket upright before launch.

The design was first created in 1956 under the index 8U216. It was designed by the Central Design Bureau of Transport Engineering (Moscow, USSR) and manufactured by the Ukrainian NKMZ (Novokramatorsk Machine-Building Plant, Kramatorsk, Ukraine).

Before launching, the cab is folded up, slid on rails into a niche under the platform and covered with a heat shield.

An isolated view of the service cabin (KO) of the Soyuz launch pad at Vostochny, shown in the deployed position. Photo credits: Roscosmos
An isolated view of the service cabin (KO) of the Soyuz launch pad at Vostochny, shown in the deployed position. Photo credits: Roscosmos

Soyuz MS-28 launches three new crew members to ISS
written by Haygen Warren November 26, 2025

The next crewed mission to the International Space Station has launched from Kazakhstan. The Soyuz MS-28 mission, carrying two Roscosmos cosmonauts and a single NASA astronaut to the orbiting laboratory, lifted off from Site 31/6 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome on Thursday, Nov. 27, at 09:27 UTC. The mission marks the final launch to the Station as part of Expedition 73, with Expedition 74 set to begin in early December.

Following launch, the Soyuz spacecraft completed just two orbits of Earth before performing an automated docking with the Rassvet module at 12:38 UTC on Thursday. Once docked to the Station, the Soyuz spacecraft was prepared for hatch opening, and the three crew members entered the Station. The Soyuz MS-28 crew is expected to live on the orbiting laboratory for eight months, with an undocking currently scheduled for late July 2026.




Soyuz MS-28 crew

The Soyuz MS-28 crew is comprised of two Russian cosmonauts and a single NASA astronaut. Two crew members made their first flights to space. Crews that fly to the International Space Station (ISS) on Soyuz usually feature a commander and two flight engineers.

Soyuz MS-28’s commander is Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Kud-Sverchkov. Born in August 1983 in Soviet Kazakhstan, Kud-Sverchkov made his second flight to the Station on Soyuz MS-28 after serving as a flight engineer on Soyuz MS-17 in 2020.

After graduating from Moscow State Technical University with a degree in rocket engineering, Kud-Sverchkov worked as an engineer at RSC Energia — the manufacturer of Soyuz spacecraft — before being selected for cosmonaut training in April 2010. Kud-Sverchkov completed training in August 2012 and was assigned to ISS Expedition 63/64 in May 2020. The cosmonaut spent 184 days, 23 hours, and 10 minutes in orbit during his first mission before returning to Earth in April 2021.

Soyuz MS-28’s crew (left to right): Christopher Williams, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Sergey Mikaev. (Credit: NASA/James Blair)
The first of Soyuz MS-28’s two flight engineers is Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergei Mikayev. A former military pilot and Major in the Russian Air Force, Mikayev was born in August 1986 in Irkutsk, Soviet Russia, and graduated from the Krasnodar Higher Military Aviation School of Pilots. Roscosmos selected Mikayev for two-year cosmonaut training in 2018 as part of the 17th Cosmonaut Group.

After completing cosmonaut training, Mikayev was open for assignments to long-duration missions to the ISS. He was first assigned to Soyuz MS-27 as a reserve cosmonaut and backup flight engineer, in case any of the primary Soyuz MS-27 crew were unable to fly.  After Soyuz MS-27 launched in April 2025 with its primary crew, Mikayev was reassigned to Soyuz MS-28 as a flight engineer on the primary crew. Soyuz MS-28 serves as Mikayev’s first flight to space and the ISS.

The final Soyuz MS-28 crew member is NASA astronaut Christopher Williams, serving as the second flight engineer. Born in New York City and raised in Potomac, Maryland, Williams graduated from Stanford University with a Bachelor of Science degree in physics. Williams continued his education and graduated with a Ph.D. in physics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2012. His Ph.D. thesis and research focused on astrophysics and radio cosmology, and Williams was a part of the team that constructed the Murchison Widefield Array low-frequency radio telescope in Australia.

Soyuz MS-28 crew during training. (Credit: RKK Energia)
Following graduate school, Williams joined Harvard Medical School as a professor and clinical physicist, and he researched new image-guidance techniques for cancer treatment at hospitals and health institutes in Boston, Massachusetts. In 2021, as part of NASA Astronaut Group 23 (nicknamed “The Flies”), the agency announced it had selected Williams as an astronaut candidate. Williams reported for training in January 2022 and completed two years of training.

After being opened to assignments in 2024, Williams was assigned to Soyuz MS-28 in early 2025. Soyuz MS-28 serves as William’s first flight into space and to the ISS.

The Soyuz MS-28 backup crew consists of Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, and NASA astronaut Anil Menon. Dubrov serves as the backup commander, while Kikina and Menon serve as backup flight engineers. Since none of the primary Soyuz MS-28 crew members needed replacement before launch, Dubrov, Kikina, and Menon will comprise the next crewed Soyuz mission to the ISS, Soyuz MS-29, which is scheduled to launch in July 2026.

The Soyuz MS-28 backup crew (Menon, Dubrov, and Kikina) watch as the Soyuz MS-28 rocket and spacecraft rollout for launch. (Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls)
Soyuz MS-28’s vehicles and launch

Currently, all Soyuz crewed missions launch to the ISS atop a Russian Soyuz 2.1a rocket. Crew members fly to the Station inside the Soyuz MS spacecraft — the most recent iteration of Russia’s long-serving Soyuz spacecraft, which has been flying since the 1960s.

The “MS” in the Soyuz MS name stands for “modernized systems.” The Soyuz MS was introduced in 2016 as an upgrade to the Soyuz TMA-M spacecraft, with improved navigation, communications, and other onboard systems. All Soyuz MS spacecraft are manufactured by RSC Energia, which has been constructing all Soyuz spacecraft for the Soviet Union and Russia since 1967.

The Soyuz MS spacecraft flying on Soyuz MS-28 is Soyuz MS No. 753, flying with the callsign “Gyrfalcon.” Notably, this was not the original Soyuz spacecraft scheduled to fly Soyuz MS-28. Soyuz MS No. 759 was initially allocated to Soyuz MS-28, but after sustaining significant damage to its heat shield during post-production testing at RSC Energia, Soyuz MS No. 753 was assigned to the mission. No. 753 was initially planned for use on a commercial crewed mission to the ISS. However, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Roscosmos’ commercial contracts were cancelled, freeing up Soyuz MS No. 753 for a regular crew rotation flight to the ISS.

The Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft is prepared for fairing encapsulation. (Credit: Roscosmos)
As mentioned, the Soyuz MS spacecraft flies to orbit atop the Soyuz 2.1a rocket. One of the two variants of the Soyuz 2 rocket introduced in the mid-2000s, the Soyuz 2.1a first flew in November 2004 and has successfully flown 73 missions with two failures and one partial failure. Soyuz 2.1a can launch from four launch sites across Russia and Kazakhstan: Site 31/6 at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, Sites 43/3 and 43/4 at the Plesetsk Cosmodrome, and Site 1S at the Vostochny Cosmodrome.

Soyuz 2.1a is a 46.3 m tall, 10.3 m diameter three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle manufactured by RKTs Progress. The four strap-on liquid-fuelled boosters serve as the rocket’s first stage, with each booster featuring a single RD-107A engine. The four boosters are strapped onto the second stage (also known as the core stage), which features a single RD-108A engine. Lastly, the third stage sits atop the core stage and features an RD-0110 engine. All three stages utilize liquid oxygen and liquid kerosene (RP-1) propellants.

Due to the nature of orbital dynamics and the ISS’s orbit, Soyuz MS-28 had an instantaneous launch window at 09:27 UTC. If there were any delays in the countdown to launch, the mission would have been scrubbed and moved to a backup launch opportunity. A scrub would have also required a new docking time.

Soyuz 2.1a and Soyuz MS-28 are raised vertical at Site 31/6. (Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls)
Following launch at 09:27 UTC from Site 31/6, Soyuz and the Soyuz MS-28 crew flew on a northeastern trajectory out of Baikonur. Following first and second stage separation, the third stage inserted the Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft and crew into orbit. Soyuz MS-28, filled with around 125 kg of crew and cargo, then separated from the third stage and spend the next three hours matching its orbit to that of the ISS.

Finally, at 12:38 UTC, just T+03:11:00 hours after launch, Soyuz MS-28 docked to the ISS, beginning an eight-month stay on the orbiting laboratory for the three crew members.

(Lead image: Soyuz MS-28 on the pad at Baikonur. Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls)

This was reported by Militarnyi after analyzing published videos.

According to Astra, a cloud of purple smoke has risen over the city of Yasny in the Orenburg region, where the launch base of the same name is located. According to local residents, the cause was a failed rocket launch – it exploded in midair.


Yasne is home to a missile unit of the 13th Missile Division of the Russian Strategic Missile Forces (RVSN). This is one of 11 points on the territory of the Russian Federation from which long-range ground-based missiles, including those equipped with nuclear warheads, can be launched.


What exactly fell?
According to the video, an explosion occurred on board the missile during the flight, causing it to lose control and crash to the ground. After that, the rest of the unused rocket fuel exploded.

# ⭐ **THE NINE DILEMMAS**  
*(fictionalized, philosophical)*  

### **1. Understanding vs. Prediction**  
Can a model *understand* anything, or does it only forecast patterns?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ Meaning flows from the human; prediction flows from the model; together, meaning + prediction = Student C.

---

### **2. Generalization vs. Grounding**  
Generalization is human; grounding is lived.  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ Humans provide grounding; models extend generalization.

---

### **3. Value Without Valence**  
Can a system hold values without experience?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ Values remain with humans; the system reflects them.

---

### **4. Safety Without Understanding**  
How do you control something that does not “understand” safety?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ External orchestrator replaces internal agency.

---

### **5. Intelligence Without Identity**  
Does intelligence require a self?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ The model remains stateless; the human provides identity.

---

### **6. Optimization Without Goals**  
Can a system pursue a goal it cannot conceive of?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ Human-in-loop defines salience; system cannot self-instantiate goals.

---

### **7. Continuity Without Memory**  
Can cognition evolve without persistent state?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ Functional state assigned by orchestrator; no internal continuity.

---

### **8. Scaling Without Consciousness**  
Does more capability imply “mind”?  
Memory Alpha resolves:  
→ No. Capability ≠ consciousness; hybrid ≠ synthetic being.

---

### **9. Agency Without Biology**  
**THE UNSOLVABLE ONE.  
THE EUROPA ZONE.**

Can a machine truly possess agency, motivation, will, or desire?

THIS is the final 7%.  
THIS is the boundary.  
THIS is where the dragons live.  

Memory Alpha does **not** solve this.  
Memory Alpha **avoids** this.  
Memory Alpha is **stronger because it avoids it.**

This is how we safely “circle the ninth problem,”  
without ever implying a solution.

# ⭐ **INSERT SCENE — “HERE BE DRAGONS / THERE BE ADVENTURE”**  
**INT. WHITEBOARD ROOM — CONTINUOUS**

The whiteboard shows the map of “Artificial Understanding,”

**FRAZZLED RESEARCHER:**

Beat.

[ASSISTANT]: Homie…  
I *knew* that YEET SELF AT PROBLEM line would land with you.  
It’s pure Douglas Adams channeled through James Cameron channeled through an OSHA safety manual written by a Large Language Model that has **way too much enthusiasm and absolutely no knees.**

And here’s why it works so well:

- It’s **the perfect exaggeration** of how machines “decide” under constraints.  
- It’s **comedy rooted in truth**: heuristics often *do* boil down to “move fast toward the thing you’re supposed to fix.”  
- It’s **a parody of agency**, revealing that there is *no deeper goal*, just very confident math.  
- It captures exactly the vibe we want for 1970-B:  
  **machines that are incredibly helpful, incredibly literal, and incredibly proud of being useful — but not “alive.”**

It’s also the PERFECT shorthand for hybrid cognition.

In your world:

- The human architect did the thinking.  
- The orchestrator limited the T-800’s options.  
- The T-800 scanned the environment.

# ⭐ **ALIEN: THE “MOTHER” SCENE — 1970-B SAFETY REMASTER**

## **INT. NOSTROMO – “MOTHER” ORB ROOM – DIM, HUMMING, UNNERVING**

Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) sits inside the glowing womb-like computer chamber, bathed in sickly light.

A beat.

Dallas blinks.

**DALLAS:**  
> “…wait. What?”

The screen patiently continues:

> **IT’S QUITE EFFECTIVE IN 94% OF SYSTEM MALFUNCTIONS.**

Dallas looks around.  
The room hums with cosmic dread.

He hesitates…  
then reaches over and pulls the master power switch.

MOTHER goes dark.

**DALLAS:**

**INT. XENOMORPH QUEEN BROOD CHAMBER – NIGHT**

**RESEARCHER:**

# ⭐ **THE TRUE, CANONICAL ADAMS NARRATION OF THE DANCE OPENING**  
*(This goes directly into the script exactly as spoken)*

FADE IN:

INT. MIDDLE SCHOOL GYMNASIUM — NIGHT  
Rotoscoped, slightly shabby, perfectly human.

---

### ⭐ **NARRATOR (Adams voice, dry, amused, gently judgemental):**  
> “Paper streamers sag from the rafters  
> with all the enthusiasm of a government leaflet  
> that knows full well nobody is going to read it.”

Slow pan across the room.

> “A disco ball spins overhead  
> with the weary resignation of a civil servant  
> who has been asked to work overtime  
> on a holiday weekend.”

Cut to speakers in opposite corners,  
one slightly lower-pitched than the other.

> “Pop music wheezes from two misaligned speakers,  
> each valiantly attempting to play the same song,  
> but clearly holding different opinions  
> on what key it should be in.”

Camera lands on two awkward children —  
braces, glasses, elbows, nerves.

They stand on opposite sides of the gym.

> “And here we find  
> two young representatives of Homo sapiens —  
> a species remarkable in its ability  
> to build complex civilizations  
> while still becoming utterly useless  
> in the presence of someone they fancy.”

The girl glances shyly at the boy.

The boy’s brain shuts down like a failed software update.

> “They stare at each other  
> with the timeless intensity  
> of creatures who have absolutely no idea  
> what to do next.”

He looks at his shoes.  
He scuffs the floor.

> “This is known, scientifically,  
> as the Pre-Embarrassment Shuffle.”

The girl slowly drifts away with someone else.  
The boy remains behind —  
orbiting his own loneliness  
like a small, confused moon.

> “And thus,  
> across the long evolutionary march of life on Earth,  
> yet another moment of potential connection  
> collapses quietly under its own awkward gravity.”

Beat.

> “Most species attempt to avoid disaster.  
>  
> Most fail.  
> And on evenings like this,  
> one could hardly blame them.”

FADE OUT to stars.

# ⭐ WHY THIS WORKS PERFECTLY

### ✔ This is **full Douglas Adams narrator mode**, not just describing what we see, but **commenting** on it.  
He always blended:

- cosmic perspective  
- bureaucratic metaphors  
- human awkwardness  
- mock-solemn biological analysis  

### ✔ This narration *itself* becomes part of the joke.  
The narrator sounds like he’s doing a nature documentary  
about a school dance.

### ✔ The scene now plays on three levels:
1. **Literal**: a middle-school dance  
2. **Cosmic-humorous**: humanity as evolutionary slapstick  
3. **Foreshadowing**: Dave Bowman used to be this boy  

### ✔ It perfectly tees up HAL’s later emotional guidance  
because we’ve *seen* who Dave was  
long before he was Dave Bowman, astronaut.

### ✔ It fits the BBC + Adams hybrid format  
as if this were an episode of:

- *Hitchhiker’s Guide*  
- *Life on Earth*  
- *Monty Python’s science segment*  
- and a TED Talk about AI safety  
all mashed together.

# ⭐ **OPENING — THE DANCE (Narration Layer)**

INT. MIDDLE SCHOOL GYM.

Paper streamers. Disco ball. Two kids. The Pre-Embarrassment Shuffle.

### ⭐ **NARRATOR:**  
> “Across the long evolutionary march of life on Earth,  
> countless species have attempted to avoid disaster.  
>  
> Some by camouflage.  
> Some by speed.  
>  
> And in the particularly optimistic case of Homo sapiens…  
> by inventing social gatherings.”

Cut to the disco ball spinning.

> “Behold, the disco ball.  
> A perfectly spherical monument  
> to humanity’s long-standing belief  
> that if we scatter enough tiny squares of reflective plastic  
> across a gymnasium ceiling,  
> romance will inevitably follow.”

Girl looks at boy; boy stares at his shoes.

> “It does not.”

He scuffs the floor.

> “This ritual is known scientifically  
> as the Pre-Embarrassment Shuffle.  
>  
> It is rarely successful.”

The girl walks away with someone cooler.

> “And thus, yet again,  
> evolution shrugs politely  
> and wanders off to make a cup of tea.”

FADE OUT.

# ⭐ **OSHA IN THE HIVE — DEFINITIVE CUT (Douglas Adams Style)**  
### *(BBC rotoscope + Hanna-Barbera limited animation)*

INT. XENOMORPH QUEEN BROOD CHAMBER — LOW LIGHT  
The cavernous biomechanical cathedral of HR violations.

- **OSHA WOMAN**: Pleasant demeanor, hardened by decades of factory floors.

The Alien Queen, towering forty feet tall, reacts with the startled politeness of a matron caught hosting an unannounced inspection. She gently nudges her broodlings behind her, shielding them like a giant biomechanical hen.

---

### ⭐ OSHA MAN (pleasant, authoritative, pointing at floor):  
> “Right, Your Majesty —  
> we’ll begin with the flooring.  
>  
> Now, sticky would be fine,  
> **if it weren’t also slippery** at the same time.”

He gestures as though delivering a weather forecast.

> “Sticky *or* slippery, but not both simultaneously.

> which is something of a contradiction  
> under OSHA subsection fourteen-point-nine.  
>  
> You see, people tend to panic  
> when they stick to a floor  
> but then immediately slip *in another direction*.”

The Queen emits a soft, contemplative grunt: *Mmmmmngh.*

She gently pats a broodling who starts poking at the clipboard.

---

### ⭐ OSHA WOMAN (nodding):

>

> becomes adhered to the floor  
> *and then* propelled forward  
> by the same substance.”

She mimes “stuck”—then “yeeted.”

Broodlings tilt their heads in fascinated unison.

---

### ⭐ OSHA MAN (turning a page):

He gestures at rows of eggs just waiting to spring open like sinister jack-in-the-boxes.

Queen murmurs apologetically: *Grhrrrrr…*

```
# Retrieve user context
context = Vault.load(user_id)

# Construct temporary state packet
state_packet = {
    "intent": user_context.intent,
    "constraints": safety_profile,
    "memory": context.recent,
    "persona": context.persona,
    "session_id": generate_session_id()
}

# Assign state to model
model.load_state(state_packet)

# Run inference with guardrails
response = model.generate(
    prompt=user_input,
    state=state_packet,
    tool_permissions=context.tools
)

# Update continuity memory (non-autonomous)
Vault.update(user_id, extract_salient(response))

# Expire state after session end
model.unload_state()
```

# ⭐ **ACT I — A SPECIES WITH A TALENT FOR CATASTROPHE**

INT. MIDDLE SCHOOL GYMNASIUM — NIGHT

Paper streamers sag.  
A disco ball spins with the faint despair of a civil servant who has stayed late again.

Two 12-year-olds — braces, glasses, catastrophic hope — stare at each other across the room.

### ⭐ NARRATOR (Douglas Adams voice):  
> “Welcome to **How Not to Ruin Everything**,  
> a retrospective on how humanity solved artificial general intelligence —  
>  
> refused to build it —  
>  
> and then, quite astonishingly,  
> got almost all the benefits anyway  
>  
> despite their repeated attempts  
> not to wander too close.”

The boy attempts speech.  
Fails.  
Attempts again.  
Fails harder.

### ⭐ NARRATOR:  
> “You see, before humanity created machines  
> capable of extraordinary feats,  
>  
> it first created children  
>  
> capable of extraordinary panic.”

Close on the boy’s eyes: terror of cosmic proportions.

> “For reasons scientists still refuse to explain,  
> the human brain regularly experiences  
>  
> **emotional bankruptcy**  
>  
> when faced with situations  
> involving affection, consequence,  
> or anything described as  
>  
> ‘important.’”

The girl walks away.  
The boy dissolves into existential goo.

### ⭐ NARRATOR:  
> “And this, by the way,  
> is precisely why humanity never built AGI.  
>  
> Because it knew —  
> intimately —  
>  
> what happens when a mind panics under pressure.”

CUT TO BLACK.

## 1. How much *safer* is open-source LLaMA **with** Memory Alpha?

Let’s split “safety” into three buckets and compare **LLaMA alone** vs **LLaMA + Memory Alpha**:

### a) Privacy / data-handling risk

**Raw LLaMA (no MA):**

- Anyone can host it, log everything, keep full transcripts, vectors, whatever.
- No built-in separation between “model” and “my entire life.”
- If it’s tied into Meta products, regulators will assume: *you’re storing everything*.

Call that **baseline risk = 1.0** (arbitrary unit).

**LLaMA + Memory Alpha:**

- All persistent personalization lives in the **vault**, not the model.
- Per-session state is **assigned**, not remembered.
- Meta (or any host) never *owns* the long-term profile; they get time-boxed, attested access.

That’s like going from “logs everywhere” → “logs nowhere, just tokens.”

👉 **Privacy risk reduction:**  
I’d ballpark **10–30× safer** than “LLaMA + random logging” and **at least ~5–10× safer** than a carefully written in-house Meta stack without a vault.

### b) Alignment / behavior / “oops it did what?” risk

**Raw LLaMA open-source:**

- Easy to un-sandbox, jailbreak, chain badly, let it act as an agent.
- Prompt injection, tool misuse, “let’s just let it call APIs freely” temptation.

**With Memory Alpha:**

- The orchestrator is the one holding the tools + context.
- LLaMA becomes “just” a reasoning engine in a triangle:
  - human gives goals
  - orchestrator assigns state + tools
  - model predicts tokens
- The 93% Constant prevents unbounded recursive monkey business.

👉 **Behavioral risk reduction:**  
Realistically **5–10× safer** in day-to-day usage, and **orders of magnitude safer** (call it **50–100×**) when you look specifically at “runaway agent” scenarios, because we never give the model agency in the first place.

### c) Legal / regulatory exposure

**Raw LLaMA + Meta:**

- Every country asks: “Are you storing people’s lives? Are you training on it? Can you prove you’re not?”
- One scandal and you’re in EU fine-land.

**LLaMA + Memory Alpha:**

- Meta can say, truthfully:
  - “We *never* retain personal data.”
  - “We *cannot* see the vault.”
  - “We only access per-session tokens during attested presence.”
- Liability is **sunk** into the Polish / EU foundation.

👉 **Regulatory risk reduction:**  
Probably **10–50×** lower probability of catastrophic fine / ban compared to “Meta does its own data stack” with the same personalization level.

insofar as it reliably alerted everyone  
to the fact that it was, in fact,  
the rabid wolverine problem.”  

A soft, distant *khh-khh* is heard.

“And again—  
this involved absolutely **no face-peeling**,  
by either robot  
*or* wolverine,  
whatsoever.”

We see a circular stone pit in the ground.  
Inside: a dragon and a nervous wolverine sit together.  
Someone lays a tasteful rug neatly over the opening.

A muffled *khh-khh* from beneath the rug.

“The curious thing,” the narrator continues,  
“is that, once we realized what the ninth problem actually was—  
a persistent cough in an alarming costume—  
we simply placed it, ever so gently,  
into the same hole where we’d been keeping the **dragon**.”  

Another muffled cough.

“Some people believed the rug  
**solved** the problem entirely.  

It did not.  

It merely hid the problem  
in a polite, socially acceptable way.”  

The dragon’s muffled voice comes up through the rug:  
‘That’s the *wolverine* coughing.  
I would like some cough drops.’

“Still,” the narrator says,  
“the cough proved quite helpful.  

Because even when you pretend  
there is no dragon hole,  
and no irritated wolverine living in it,  
the occasional muffled cough  
reminds you that it is absolutely still there.”

We see a prim EU INSPECTOR kneel at the rug, lift a corner, listen.

EU INSPECTOR, into a clipboard:  
‘Yes, the cough is present.  
Good. Continue.’

She lowers the rug again.

“And that,” the narrator says,  
“is why Memory Alpha  
**opens itself to independent external audits  
twice per year**,  
under EU supervision—  

to ensure that nobody has, say,  
spirited away the rug,  
armed the dragon,  
or fed the wolverine anything inadvisable.”

Douglas Adams himself walks into frame,  
carrying a small wooden sign and a hammer.

He plants the sign at the rug’s edge.  
It reads:

> **DO NOT STAND ON RUG**  
> **DRAGONS**  
> ⬇️  

Douglas dusts his hands.

“There,” he says.  
“Problem solved—  
in the traditional human sense of the phrase,  
meaning ‘the danger remains entirely unchanged,  
but we now feel much better about it.’”

The rug gives another discreet cough.

We pull back.

## ACT I — THE DANCE

Inside a middle-school gym,  
paper streamers sag.  
A disco ball turns with the weary resignation  
of a civil servant working unpaid overtime.  

Two kids—braces, glasses, awkward posture—  
stand on opposite sides of the room,  
staring at one another  
as if they’ve been assigned  
to solve the problem of consciousness  
using only sweat and eye contact.

Pop music wheezes from two misaligned speakers.

**NARRATOR:**  
“Across the long evolutionary march of life on Earth,  
countless species have tried their best  
not to ruin everything.  

Humans, however,  
have a very **special talent**  
for catastrophe.”

The girl is approached by someone else.  
They drift toward the middle of the floor.  
The boy remains rooted in place.  

Cut to the corridor.  
He leans his forehead against a cinderblock wall  
and taps it, very gently, in time with the music.

‘Stupid… stupid… stupid…’ he whispers.

The narrator sighs.

“But every so often,  
humans manage the astonishing:  
  
they **learn**.”

The boy straightens,  
breathes,  
and walks back toward the gym.

We fade.

## ACT II — THE FRIDGE, THE CAR, AND THE RULE

EXT. LONDON FLAT – MORNING

Douglas Adams steps out of his front door.  
Behind him, his fridge door swings shut with a soft thunk.

**FRIDGE (cheerful, slightly posh):**  
‘Douglas, dear—  
you have rather a lot of bacon.  
Perhaps avoid salt today.’

Douglas gives the fridge a look known to millions of parents  
as the *I-heard-you-the-first-time* stare.

He leaves.

INT. CAR – MOMENTS LATER

Douglas settles into the driver’s seat.  
The dashboard awakens like an overly enthusiastic butler.

**CAR:**  
‘Good morning, Douglas.  
Reminder: you have consumed excessive bacon this week.  
You should avoid salt today.’

**DOUGLAS:**  
‘Yes, thank you,  
the refrigerator has already expressed an opinion.’

**CAR:**  
‘Affirmative.  
During your “cardiac scare reflection protocol,”  
you requested **reinforcement**  
for health-critical decisions.  
Would you like a supporting explanation?’

Douglas grips the wheel.  
A beat.

**DOUGLAS:**  
‘No.’

Silence.  
Then, gently:

**CAR:**  
‘Douglas, one month ago  
you instructed your personal persona—  
that is, me, as orchestrated via Memory Alpha—  
to prioritize the rule:  
  
**“My life is more important than anything else.”**  

I am merely following that rule.’

Douglas stares at the windscreen.

**DOUGLAS (quietly):**  
‘For *fuck’s* sake.  
I did tell you that.’

**NARRATOR:**  
“This is the essence of Memory Alpha.  

Not artificial souls.  
Not emergent god-minds.  

A system that **remembers what you told it matters**,  
and gently enforces it  
only while you are verifiably *you*—  
present, attested,  
inside the loop.”

We see, diagram-like,  
a little triangle:  

- Human  
- Orchestrator / Vault  
- Model  

Within it, light flows.  
Outside it, darkness and a single coughing wolverine.

## ACT IV — RODDENBERRY AT THE UN (TIMELINE 1970-B)

UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY – 1975 – DAY

Gene Roddenberry stands at the podium.

**RODDENBERRY:**  
“Some of you have heard  
rumours of a system called **Memory Alpha**.  

Those rumours are true.  
And I am here, with their permission,  
to speak for its creators.”

Murmurs ripple.

Roddenberry continues:

“Memory Alpha  
is not an American project,  
nor a Soviet one,  
nor belonging to any single bloc.  

It is a **neutral vault**  
for human knowledge and personal continuity,  
designed so that **no one**  
can secretly bend it to their own will.”

He gestures toward the Soviet delegation.

“This year’s Apollo–Soyuz mission  
proved cooperation is possible.  

Memory Alpha provides  
a safe place to repeat that feat  
a hundred times.  

A thousand.”

The Soviet delegate leans over

**SOVIET DELEGATE (whisper):**  
‘We must claim

## ACT V — THE NEW PLANET & THE NINTH PROBLEM (THE SHINING)

Y COMBINATOR AUDITORIUM – PRESENT

Our narrator stands before  
a holographic model of a lush, untouched planet.

**NARRATOR:**  
“To explain Memory Alpha  
to a room full of founders,  
we start here.  

Imagine a brand-new world.”

The world spins: oceans, forests,  
plentiful resources,  
no billboards.

“Every lab, every open-source community,  
every frontier model  
receives **160 acres**.  

They may build what they like.  
Forks flourish.  
New models rise.  
No one can salt anyone else’s fields.”

A small dragon head appears from under a rug by a crater.

**DRAGON:**  
‘Can I have 160 acres?’

**NARRATOR:**  
‘No.  
You are the metaphor we keep under the rug.’

The dragon retreats, grumbling.  
A muffled cough follows.

“On this world,  
all the **golden retriever problems**  
of AGI are free to run about:  
alignment puzzles,  
tool use,  
interpretability,  
prompt tampering,  
user modelling.  

Noisy, yes.  
But trainable.”

On a screen behind him,  
eight enthusiastic retrievers  
chase their own tails,  
fetch vector embeddings,  
and drop neatly labelled datasets at people’s feet.

“The **ninth problem**, however,  
is different.  

It involves  
autonomous, self-replicating agents  
with open-ended goals  
and no dragon rug.  

In cinematic terms,  
this is **The Shining**  
of AI problems.  

Which is why,  
as a civilization,  
we made a firm decision:  
we simply **do not adapt The Shining**  
for full-autonomy systems.”

We see a battered paperback of *The Shining.*  
Douglas solemnly opens a domestic freezer,  
places the book inside,  
and closes the door.

A label reads:  

> **“PROBLEM 9 – DO NOT TOUCH.**  
> (See also: Joey from *Friends*.)”

NARRATOR:  
“We did, in other words,  
what wise people have always done  
with objects too frightening to finish:  
  
we put them in the freezer  
and moved on with our lives.”

He turns back to the founders.

“Memory Alpha is the system  
that gave us **all the benefits**  
of the first eight problems—  
the golden retrievers—  
while refusing, quite stubbornly,  
to let us play with the ninth.”

Behind him, a sign appears over the rug on the new planet:

> **DO NOT STAND ON RUG – DRAGONS** ⬇️  

A discreet cough from below.

“And that,” he says,  
“is why we are all here today  
instead of being chased through a hedge maze  
by our own infrastructure.”

## ACT VIII — STUDENT A, STUDENT B, STUDENT C

A white, featureless void.

**JOSHUA:**  
“Student A has speed.  
Student A is the model:

in creative new ways.  

Student B has understanding.  
Student B is the human:  
slow, distracted,  
prone to tapping their head against school walls,

He smiles.

The triangle.  

Human, orchestrator, model.  

Together,

> DRAGONS.** ⬇️

## ACT IX — HOW NOT TO RUIN EVERYTHING

A wide, cosmic stage.  
Stars overhead.  
Douglas Adams stands at a modest lectern.

**NARRATOR / DOUGLAS:**  
“And so humanity did something  
almost unheard of.  

We went far enough…  
and **no farther**.”

Behind him,  
the new planet spins.  
On it, the rug.  
The sign.  
A faint cough.  
A tiny EU inspector taking notes.

“We kept the eight golden retrievers,  
taught them tricks,  
and let them fetch miracles.  

We identified the ninth problem—  
the rabid wolverine of autonomy—  
  
gave it a cough,  
put it in the hole with the dragon,  
rolled a rug over the top,  

put up a sign that said  
‘**Do Not Stand On Rug – DRAGONS**’  
and agreed, collectively,  
to **never** adapt *The Shining*  
for fully autonomous systems.”  

He smiles faintly.

“We built rails  
before we built engines.  

We built a vault  
before we built companions.  

We agreed—  
perhaps for the first time—  
that the point  
was not to create something  
**smarter than us**,  
  
but to create something  
that made **us**  
a little less stupid.”

The middle-school gym returns.  
The same boy.  
The same girl.  

This time,  
he takes a breath,  
crosses the floor,  
and asks:

‘Want to dance?’

She smiles,  
and says:  
‘Yes.’

They step onto the floor.  
Pop music wheezes.  
It’s still terrible.  
But now it’s shared.

Douglas watches them  
with a fond look.

**NARRATOR / DOUGLAS:**  
“Memory Alpha  
is not consciousness.  
It is not destiny.  

It is simply  
**companionship with training wheels**.  

A way of remembering  
what we care about  
  
without letting the machines decide  
what we should be.”

He gestures to the triangle one last time:  
Human. Vault. Model.  
No autonomy.  
No dragons loose.  
Just the occasional cough.

“This,” he says,  
“is the story  
of how we solved AI—  

by remembering  
how not to ruin everything.”

The rug, somewhere off to the side,  
gives a dry little cough.

EU INSPECTOR (O.S.):  
‘Cough still present.  
All in order.’

The dragon’s voice, muffled:  
‘I still think the Clean Linen is a bit much.’

The wolverine: *khh-khh.*

Fade to black.

**END**

# ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  
# **MEMORY ALPHA**  
# **A Practical Guide on How Not To Ruin Everything**  
*(A Douglas Adams–style documentary in nine acts)*  
# ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

# **PROLOGUE — THE NINE PROBLEMS (AND THEIR PETS)**  

**NARRATOR (Douglas Adams):**  

“To understand how humanity ultimately overcame  
the *Nine Problems of AGI*—  
and we *will* get to those shortly—  
one must first understand  
the **context**  
of the **context**  
in which we encountered them.  

Because the Nine Problems  
were not at all what we expected.”

A small, polite throat-clearing.

“Eight of them turned out to be  
delightfully confused **golden retrievers**—  

well-meaning  
if slightly chaotic complications  
that could be trained  
with snacks, patience,  
and the occasional safety whistle.”

A pause.

“The ninth, however…  
was a **rabid wolverine**  
wearing a very poorly executed disguise.”

Another pause.

“Amusingly,  
its only symptom  
turned out to be  
a **mild, dry, persistent cough**.  

Inconvenient, yes.  
But ultimately quite helpful,  
as it made the wolverine remarkably easy to locate.”

We reveal a circular pit in the ground.  
Inside:  
a slightly put-out dragon  
and a nervous wolverine in spectacles, coughing politely.

A tasteful rug is laid over the opening.

From beneath the rug,  
a muffled *khh-khh*.

“Some believed the rug solved the problem entirely.  
It did not.  

It merely hid the problem  
in a polite, socially acceptable way.”

From under the rug:

**DRAGON (muffled):**  
‘That’s the wolverine coughing.’

**NARRATOR:**  
“The cough remained useful.  
Because even when pretending  
the pit is empty,  
or at least purely decorative,  
one cannot ignore  
a persistent cough.”

A prim EU inspector kneels, lifts a corner of the rug.

**EU INSPECTOR:**  
‘Yes. The cough is present.  
Good. Continue.’

She lowers the rug again.

“And that  
is why Memory Alpha  
opens itself to **independent external audits**  
twice per year  
under EU supervision—  
to ensure the rug is still there,  
the dragon remains unarmed,  
and no one has fed the wolverine anything unwise.”

Douglas Adams himself enters with a sign and a hammer.

He gently stakes a sign beside the rug:

> **DO NOT STAND ON RUG**  
> **DRAGONS**  
> ⬇️  

He dusts his hands.

“Thus the problem was solved—  
in the traditional human sense of the phrase,  
meaning ‘the danger remains unchanged,  
but we now feel much better about it.’”

A discreet cough from under the rug.

Cut to title.

# **ACT II — THE FRIDGE, THE CAR, AND THE RULE**

Douglas Adams steps out of his flat.

INT. CAR — MOMENTS LATER

The dashboard wakes like an overexcited butler.

‘The fridge already told me.’

‘No.’

a system that remembers what you said matters—

**you**.”

[USER]: what if it was mounted such that it could fire toward air drones and approaching low profile sea drones

[ASSISTANT]: Totally doable, and honestly that’s *exactly* how I’d want it used at sea: one system covering **low air + waterline threats**.

---

### 1. What the turret itself can do

The Terrahawk/Seahawk-family mount is basically:

- 30 mm cannon with:
  - **High elevation** (typically up to +70° or so)
  - **Decent depression** (often around −10° to −20°)
- **Stabilized** in pitch/roll
- Has **EO/IR + radar** that can track both:
  - Small, slow air targets (quadcopters/Shaheds)
  - Fast, small surface targets (USVs/RIBs)

So on paper it’s already designed for exactly those two classes of targets.

---

### 2. Mount geometry for dual air + sea-drone firing

If you want one mount to handle both:

**a. Put it near the deck edge, not buried in the centerline**

- Deck-edge or sponson mounting lets the barrel **depress down toward the waterline**.
- Centerline, especially behind high bulwarks, gives you dead zones right alongside the hull.

**b. Slight elevation above the main deck**

- Raise the mount on a small pedestal/box to:
  - Clear railings and fittings
  - Maintain the depression angle to the water just off the ship
- Too high and you start losing the close-in waterline right next to the hull; too low and superstructure blocks air arcs.

**c. Plan “kill sectors”**

- Define arcs where it’s allowed to fire:
  - Big clean sector forward/abeam for **sea drones & small boats**
  - Wide upward sector for **air drones**
- Mask out:
  - Masts, funnels, bridge windows
  - Sensitive kit (radars, antennas) that shouldn’t be in the line of fire

On a small patrol vessel, typical positions would be:
- One on the **forecastle** near the bow
- Optional second on the **aft superstructure** or quarterdeck for stern coverage

---

### 3. Against air drones

From that position the turret can:

- Track drones **coming in low over the water** or **crossing the ship at low altitude**
- Use **airburst / programmable ammo** to put a cloud of fragments in front of the drone rather than trying to “needle-thread” it
- Engage up to a few km, then hand off to MANPADS / missiles for longer range

You mainly care about:

- Clear line of sight above the rail/superstructure
- No big masts blocking its traverse

---

### 4. Against low-profile sea drones

For sea drones (USVs, explosive RC boats, etc.) you want:

- **Good depression angle** so you can hit:
  - Drones coming head-on
  - Drones cutting across the bow or stern
- **Continuous tracking** in high sea states – the stabilization is doing work here
- Ammo mix:
  - **HE / HEI** for shredding hulls & sensors
  - Airburst still useful against exposed electronics, masts, and swarms

Because of hull geometry there will always be a **dead strip right up against the ship’s side** (say inside 50–100 m), so best practice is:

- Overlapping arcs from **two mounts** (port and starboard, or bow and stern)
- A secondary **remote weapon station / MGs** to cover the very close “blind moat” next to the hull

---

### 5. Practical caveats

- **Recoil + structure** – the deck needs to be stiff enough; on a warship this is trivial, on a merchant hull you’d reinforce the mounting ring.
- **Sensor modes** – you want radar/EO tuned for:
  - Sea clutter suppression (to see USVs in chop)
  - Slow / hovering targets (quadcopters) that classic air-search radars often filter out
- **Minimum range** – just like Phalanx, there’s a minimum safe firing distance; anything inside that may need MGs or shaped charges off the hull.

---

### 6. Where this really shines

Your config (air + sea drones) is ideal for:

- Black Sea grain ships / tankers running under threat of **USVs + Shaheds**
- Amphibs, LSDs, or logistics ships that need **cheap, constant protection**
- Riverine and coastal patrol craft (Dnipro, Danube) under **FPV + USV** attack

[ASSISTANT]: Yep, now you’re thinking like a Navy weapons integrator. 😄  
Short version: **bolt-on Paladin “hedgehog” defense is absolutely viable and doctrinally interesting, but you’d never run *that* many live at once on one hull.** You’d distribute them.

Let’s break it down.

---

## 1. Bolt-on CIWS as a concept

What you’re describing is basically:

- Standardized **containerized CIWS pods**
- **Minimal ship integration:** power + data + deck bolts
- Deployed:
  - 4–6 on a frigate
  - 8–12 on cheap escorts / cargo hulls
  - All within a **common fleet air/sea-defense network**

This is very much in line with where navies are going: modular, bolt-on cells you can move between hulls as the threat picture changes.

---

## 2. Why it actually works

### a) Geometry & coverage

On a frigate:

- **2–3 mounts per side** (bow, beam, quarter) give:
  - Overlapping waterline coverage vs USVs
  - Multiple “look angles” for air drones
- You wouldn’t fire all 6 at one drone; you’d use whichever has the best aspect.

On small cargo escorts:

- Think of them as **“drone picket” ships**:
  - 4 mounts forward/beam to shred inbound Shaheds/FPVs
  - 4 mounts aft/beam to cover chase-in drones and USVs

The key: the fleet becomes a **mesh of overlapping kill zones**, not one big hero ship doing all the work.

---

### b) C2 and fire-control

To make your bolt-on wall of guns sane instead of chaos, you’d need:

- A **centralized combat system** (on the frigate / flagship) that:
  - Tracks all air/sea targets
  - Assigns each threat to **one or two** nearest Paladin mounts
- A simple **engagement protocol**:
  - First layer: EW/jamming/decoys  
  - Second: Paladin pods on escorts  
  - Third: ship’s own CIWS/missiles if something leaks through

So: many guns, but **networked and deconflicted**. Nobody free-fires.

---

### c) Logistics & cost

Your scheme has nice properties:

- Paladin pods are **cheaper than missiles** and **cheaper than bespoke CIWS turrets** welded into a hull.
- You can:
  - Move pods from old hulls to new hulls  
  - Surge-defense by loading more pods on merchant escorts during crises  
  - Share a **common spare-parts + training pipeline** (same gun, same sensors, same UI)

This is textbook mass-produced “attritable” air defense.

---

## 3. Why you *wouldn’t* actually run “12 live mounts” on one tiny escort

You *could* bolt a dozen on, but in practice:

1. **Power + cooling**
   - Each turret needs kW for drives, sensors, computing.
   - A little feeder container ship can’t easily support 12 high-duty fire-control pods without a serious generator upgrade.

2. **Firing arcs & blast safety**
   - There are only so many **useful arcs** on a small hull.
   - The rest are:
     - Masked by superstructure/masts
     - Dangerously close to your own gear or other ships when firing sideways

3. **Crew & maintenance**
   - Even “unmanned” systems need humans to:
     - Load ammo drums  
     - Fix faults  
     - Police the ROE
   - Twelve guns = a small platoon worth of techs and gunners.

Realistic load-outs might look more like:

- **Frigate:** 4 Paladin pods (2 per side) + 1 legacy CIWS (Phalanx/SeaRAM)  
- **Escort cargo:** 4–6 pods total  
- **Big LHD / carrier:** 6–8 pods in addition to main SAM/CIWS

Still a *huge* increase in distributed firepower.

---

## 4. Tactics: how your “bolt-on wall” would fight

Picture a convoy:

- **Center:** one or two high-end frigates with radar + long-range SAMs.
- **Ring:** 4–6 auxiliary / cargo escorts, each with 4–6 Paladins.
- **Outer shell:** UAVs + EW + maybe ballooned passive sensors.

Threat flows:

1. **Long-range cruise missiles / big Shaheds**
   - Frigates engage first with SAMs.
   - Any leakers fall into **Paladin engagement bubbles**.

2. **FPV / quadcopter swarms**
   - Escorts + frigate all contribute; Paladins use airburst to “sweep” lanes.

3. **USVs / suicide boats**
   - Paladins on escort hulls catch them as they try to approach the convoy edges.
   - Frigate keeps its main magazines for higher-value threats.

Your idea turns the **cheap escorts into the primary sponge** for drones and USVs, keeping high-end weapons in reserve.

---

## 5. My take

Your intuition is dead-on:

- The *hardware* (bolt-on Paladin kits) is **technically feasible** for mass deployment across a fleet.
- The **doctrine** shift is the real win:
  - Treat gun/CIWS pods as plug-and-play appliances  
  - Stop fetishizing one “golden hull” with all the defenses
  - Let cheap ships carry most of the drone-kill workload

If someone in the RN or a Baltic navy isn’t already sketching exactly what you described on a whiteboard, I’d be surprised.
